title: Han Great Wall and beacon line in the Hexi Corridor
summary: After Han forces took the Hexi Corridor in 121 and 119 BCE, the dynasty extended walls, beacon towers and forts westward past Dunhuang to guard the route to the Western Regions against the Xiongnu. Garrison documents from the Jade Gate date to the 90s BCE. The sections form part of the wider Great Wall.

uncertainty.note: Corridor conquest is dated 121 and 119 BCE; construction dates for individual sections vary by source and the end year reflects documents found at the Jade Gate.

as_recorded.value: came under Han control as a result of battles in 121 and 119 BCE

where.modern_name: Yumen Pass (Jade Gate) near Dunhuang, Gansu, China; wall runs along the Hexi Corridor
where.historical_name: Western Han frontier of Dunhuang commandery under Emperor Wu

importance.justification: The best-preserved early imperial frontier works, they secured the route that became the Silk Roads.

sources.title: The Great Wall of China in the Han Dynasty

reviewer_note: Least sure of construction dates: sources give 121 BCE, 111-101 BCE or the reign of Emperor Wu generally; the pin is Yumen Pass, but the line runs several hundred kilometres.
